#5

It's still ok to enjoy programming

It's still ok to enjoy programming

696 分 635 评论 最高 #67 5 次快照出现
  • Published: 2026-10-17 Reading Hacker News makes me feel like I need to write this: it's still OK to enjoy programming. Yes, at work, where you are paid to produce value for a business, the economics of purely hand-written code have changed. But that's work. Work is not life. The loudest voices on the internet are the saddest and most infectious. To throw a tiny counter example in the sea of despair: I still program on the weekends because it is fun. I'm currently learning game programming! My current level of sophistication is a buggy Breakout clone with terrible collision detection. I write it by hand because I enjoy it. I struggle with problems because solving them makes me happy. It doesn't bother me that Claude could one-shot it, because that's not the point. I also get side-tracked from working on this "game" to study random programming topics. Last weekend was exploring how far I could push type safety in Java using ideas from dependently typed languages like Agda. There is no point to this. It gets tucked away under "interesting ways of thinking about a particular problem." Maybe it will come up in work life. Maybe not. I did it because exploring is was fun[0]. A few weekends ago: recursion schemes. Technically, this was not fun. I spent hours of banging my head against a wall. In the end, I still don't even know what's valuable about the ideas[1]. But I do know that many of the most beautiful ideas in programming only become clear to me after years of baking in my mind. It's why entire papers get written about Monoids. Maybe one day I'll find a problem that this applies to. Maybe not. I did it because understanding hard things is rewarding. I write this because I increasingly feel a strange social pressure. It's like I'm not "supposed" to enjoy this any more. As though there's no point or joy to be had in continuing to grow as a human. The more of this doom stream you consume, the more it starts to infect you. Maybe "there is no point," you find yourself thinking. But this disappears as soon as you disconnect.It's OK to enjoy things[2]. Doing so requires no economic justification. Footnotes: [0] Take the time to understand Fin one day. It is beautiful. [1] I'm not there yet, but the goal of studying this is to give myself another tool for reasoning about program correctness algebraically (a topic I cover in my book!) [2] I also have a blast vibe-coding. I've got a suite of apps for which I've never looked at a line of code. I suspect doing so would horrify me. "Programming" this way is also fun. Often extremely so. But in its own unique way.

The 1.5°C goal of the Paris Agreement is no longer viable

The 1.5°C goal of the Paris Agreement is no longer viable

539 分 617 评论 最高 #9 2 次快照出现
  • The target set in 2015 by the Paris Agreement—to limit global warming to 1.5°C by 2100—has become unachievable within the span of a single decade, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) notes in its 2026 Emissions Gap Report. “The opportunity to bridge the 1.5°C emissions gap with ‘no or limited’ overshoot has been lost,” states the report, titled “The Point of Return.” Exceeding the 1.5°C threshold above pre-industrial levels is now imminent and inevitable. New goal: not exceed 2°C, then bring the temperature back down to 1.5°C “Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5°C raises the risk of irreversible changes including in ice sheets, permafrost carbon, ocean circulation and coral systems, along with devastating human impacts,” the report states. The urgent task is to ensure that global warming remains below the 2°C threshold, with the aim of returning to 1.5°C by the end of the century. This is the only option left, according to UNEP.
  • © Maxim Tolchinskiy / Unsplash Highly inadequate climate plans To achieve this, global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions would need to be reduced by 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035, and 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels. The current trajectory falls far short of this. Even assuming that the commitments made by governments—known as nationally determined contributions (NDCs)—are fully implemented, emissions would only be reduced by 5% to 8% by 2030 and by 11% to 15% by 2035, compared to 2025 levels. The recommended efforts are “close to 6 per cent every single year until 2035,” declares the UN Secretary General. How can this be achieved? The UN Chief outlined the levers for action available to humanity: “The emissions gap is now a leadership gap. And the world is running out of time and excuses to close it. Governments must go much further and faster. Accelerate clean energy and electrification across every sector. Adopt credible roadmaps to transition away from fossil fuels – with clear timelines and protection for affected workers and communities. Invest in grids and storage. Improve energy efficiency. Cut methane emissions. Halt and reverse deforestation.”
